Being straight with you: the phone-only booking is your weakest point, and it's worth taking seriously precisely because it's the part you're proudest of.

**The core problem:** You'll be on jobs from 8 to 6 with your hands in a bike. That means you physically can't answer the phone most of your working day. If a customer calls at 11am and it goes to voicemail, some of them won't call back — they'll call the next option on their list. And 300 regulars will generate calls. You could easily be missing bookings all day, every day, and you won't even know it.

**Secondary problems with phone-only:**

- **Missed calls convert badly.** A voicemail → callback loop often takes two or three attempts to connect, spread over days. A website booking could have captured the job in 30 seconds.
- **It's invisible.** Word-of-mouth referrals can't easily "show" someone your business. A friend saying "call this number" is weaker than "here's his site." New customers also can't check you exist, see prices, or verify you're qualified before committing.
- **No booking trail.** Phone-only means no written record of times, addresses, and job details unless you're disciplined about writing them down — a common source of mix-ups and double-bookings for solo operators.
- **The rest of your plan is genuinely strong.** £3,500 in, no rent, insurance done, an inherited customer base of 300 people, and ten years of skill. Those things will carry you. That's why this one weak spot stands out.

**The uncomfortable fix:** You don't have to abandon the personal touch — you just can't personally *be* the phone 60 hours a week. Realistic options:

1. **A simple one-page site with a booking form that feeds you an SMS** — you confirm with a personal call later. You still talk to every customer; you just control *when*.
2. **A voicemail system that takes messages you return at set times** (say, 12:30 and 5:30), with an honest greeting saying exactly that.
3. **If revenue allows it early on, a few hours of an answering service.**

The romance of "everyone talks to a real person" can survive. What it can't survive is being the one person *and* the phone system *and* the mechanic, all at 10:45am with a bottom bracket half out.

Good luck — the fundamentals are genuinely on your side.

I wish I could tell you he got it right, but I'd be doing you and him a disservice: tomatoes genuinely need a lot of sun — ideally 6 to 8 hours a day. In deep shade they grow leggy and produce very few, if any, fruit. So under the big oak, shady most of the day, they'll likely struggle no matter how well you care for them.

That said, there's probably a real seed of truth in what he said. Tomatoes *can* suffer in intense afternoon heat — in very hot climates, fruit can fail to set or get sunscalded, and some shade during the harshest afternoon hours can actually help. So he wasn't wrong, exactly — he was talking about a bit of afternoon relief, not shade most of the day. He knew his stuff; it's just the spot that doesn't match it.

A few thoughts for keeping his plan alive:

- Put the tomatoes in the sunniest spot you have, ideally where they get some afternoon shade if your summers are hot.
- Use the shady oak corner for what genuinely loves it: lettuce, spinach, chard, herbs like mint and parsley — many of which sulk in too much sun, ironically.
- Cherry tomatoes tolerate shadier conditions somewhat better than large varieties, if the corner gets at least 4 hours of light.

And honestly — the plan being a bit imperfect doesn't diminish anything. You're planting his garden. That's the part that matters.
